name: Redox OS
summary: Free Unix-type operating system founded on a modern microkernel architecture and written in Rust, running all drivers in user space and using the RedoxFS file system.

content.introduction: Redox OS is a free, general-purpose Unix-type operating system designed around an innovative microkernel architecture. Initiated in 2015 by Jeremy Soller, the project aims to rethink the foundations of modern operating systems by taking advantage of the strict guarantees of memory safety, lock-free concurrency and strong typing offered by the Rust programming language, while drawing inspiration from the principles of architectural elegance of MINIX, seL4 and Plan 9.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Redox OS stands clearly apart from conventional monolithic systems (Linux, BSD, Windows NT). Its kernel manages only the irreducible primitive functions of the system in privileged mode (Ring 0). All device drivers, file systems and the TCP/IP network stack are moved into user space (Ring 3) as autonomous and unprivileged processes. Communication between these components takes place by means of standardised inter-process call mechanisms based on a unified URI syntax.
content.microkernel_architecture_and_user_space_: The Redox OS microkernel is strictly limited to preemptive thread scheduling, management of virtual address spaces (memory paging) and IPC communication channels. This drastic reduction of the privileged code surface strengthens operational resilience: the unforeseen failure or the crash of a disk, network card or file system driver causes no kernel panic. The faulty process can be isolated, stopped and restarted at runtime by service supervision monitors without affecting the operation of the rest of the machine.
content.paradigm_everything_is_an_url_and_redoxf: Pushing further the historical Unix maxim ("everything is a file") and the distributed vision of Plan 9, Redox OS adopts the "everything is a URL" paradigm. Interactions with hardware and software resources are expressed through standardised URI schemes (`file:`, `tcp:`, `orbital:`, `audio:`). Applications read from and write to these schemes through the standard system calls (`open`, `read`, `write`). The native file system of the platform is **RedoxFS**, a transactional copy-on-write file system inspired by the concepts of ZFS, guaranteeing block integrity through checksums and total resilience to power failures.
content.relibc_posix_compatibility_and_orbital_g: To reconcile the innovation of the Rust language with the existing software library of the Unix world, Redox OS has developed **relibc**, a portable standard C library written entirely in Rust. Designed to replace glibc or musl while eliminating the memory corruption vulnerabilities specific to the C language, relibc offers the POSIX interfaces essential for porting compilers, command-line utilities and interpreters (Python, Git, Bash, Rust). The visual environment is handled by **Orbital**, a lightweight display server and window manager written in Rust, capable of running native graphical applications and components from the modern COSMIC desktop environment.
content.hardware_support_and_project_maturity: Redox OS supports the x86-64 architecture as its reference platform, alongside images for 32-bit x86 (i586) and work in progress for AArch64 (ARM64) and RISC-V. Although perfectly functional within hypervisors such as QEMU and capable of booting on certain compatible physical computers (notably System76 machines), Redox OS officially remains at the **Alpha** development stage. Formal security guarantees and support for the most complex hardware peripherals (modern 3D acceleration, fine-grained Wi-Fi management) remain under active development. The system is distributed under the free and permissive MIT licence.
content.releases_and_community: The official website shows Redox OS 0.9.0 as the current version and refers to release notes. The project describes itself as a community active since 2015, hosts its code on a self-hosted GitLab server and has organised a Redox Summer of Code every year since 2018. Funding is presented as resting on donations (Donorbox, Patreon, Bitcoin, Ethereum) and on the sale of merchandise; the exchange channels cited are Matrix and the project's GitLab.
content.kernel_size_and_isolation_model: The project manual estimates the kernel at about 50,000 lines of code, a figure it presents as often decreasing, and describes an architecture inspired by MINIX and seL4. System services and drivers run in user space according to the principle of least authority: each component is isolated in a separate process, its failure does not cause that of the others and it has no administrative privileges. The relibc library provides the POSIX functions on the user side.
content.hardware_support_matrix: The manual lists the supported architectures: x86-64, 32-bit x86 from a Pentium II with limitations, AMD 32 and 64 bits, AArch64 with limitations and RISC-V 64 bits (riscv64gc) with limitations. The hardware interfaces cited are ACPI, PCI and USB; storage covers IDE (PATA), SATA (AHCI) and NVMe; display goes through VESA, UEFI GOP or Intel GPUs; sound, PS/2 and USB input and Intel and Realtek Ethernet cards are also documented.
content.installation_profiles_and_encryption: The installer offers four profiles: Desktop (installation announced at around 200 seconds), Server (around 90 seconds), Clone from a live disk and installation in live mode by default. It makes it possible to write to a whole disk, to a raw RedoxFS partition or into an image file, and to define an encryption password for the main RedoxFS partition: encryption covers the whole disk and the password is requested by the bootloader at startup.
content.package_management_pkgar: Package management relies on pkgar: each package is described by a header and metadata verified by BLAKE3 hash, only the modified files are downloaded during an update, then moved atomically to avoid installing invalid data. A verification procedure compares the recorded metadata with the installed files and makes it possible to rebuild a package from an existing system. The manual indicates that the repository format is still under study.
advantages: Modern microkernel architecture isolating device drivers and file systems in user space.
Native memory safety and elimination of memory corruption vulnerabilities thanks to the Rust language.
Remarkable resilience to driver failures: possibility of restarting a crashed driver without a kernel crash.
Modern RedoxFS copy-on-write file system guaranteeing the transactional integrity of data.
Elegant and unified URI paradigm ("everything is a URL") simplifying inter-process communication interfaces.
Portable standard C library `relibc` written in Rust ensuring compatibility with existing POSIX software.
disadvantages: System still officially in the Alpha development phase, with basic features being stabilised.
Physical hardware support still partial, requiring specific hardware configurations or the use of QEMU.
Native application catalogue still being built compared with operating systems established for several decades.
Inter-process communication (IPC) inherent to microkernel architectures can introduce latency overheads compared with a monolithic kernel.
Absence of full hardware 3D graphics acceleration for contemporary graphics cards.
who_is_it_for: Researchers, operating system architects and enthusiasts exploring the future of secure microkernel architectures.
Developers of the Rust ecosystem wishing to study or contribute to a modern operating system written entirely in Rust.
Critical systems and embedded computing engineers looking for high-level hardware and software isolation.
Advanced users wishing to experiment with innovative software engineering concepts within virtual machines.
who_is_it_not_for: General public users looking for a desktop system ready for daily production on their personal computer.
PC video game players requiring advanced DirectX 12 / Vulkan libraries and closed graphics drivers.
Enterprises requiring formal industrial certifications, service level agreements (SLA) or 24/7 support.
Production infrastructures requiring massive deployments of Linux containers or heavy distributed databases.
content.verdict: Redox OS is an experimental operating system project. By combining the memory guarantees of the Rust language with the microkernel architecture, it explores an alternative to monolithic systems written in C.
content.origine_et_chronologie_du_projet:
The chronology established by the project's sources begins with the creation of the main repository. The hosting service API gives a creation date of 2015-04-20 for the redox-os/redox repository; this is the only founding date verifiable in the sources consulted. No page of the documentation book gives a founding date, a founder's name or a first publication date; this limit is recorded as such.

The project publishes a monthly chronicle entitled "This Month in Redox", whose last consultable issue is dated 2026-08-31. This chronicle documents the evolution of the system month by month: driver integration, progress of software porting, state of RedoxFS. On 2025-09-12, the project published a text entitled "Development Priorities for 2025/26", which sets out the priority work of the period. The topics of the 2026 edition of the development grant programme, Redox Summer of Code, are also published on the same thread.

The book sets out the motivation of the project on a dedicated page: a microkernel, partial restarts of services, a RedoxFS file system presented as comparable to ZFS, and a POSIX API provided by relibc making it possible to port software by recompilation. These elements explain the technical direction followed between 2015 and 2026, without constituting a dated history of versions, which the sources consulted do not provide.

components.name: Redox kernel
components.note: "The Redox kernel is a microkernel." (Microkernels); the chapter on the Redox kernel documents the system-call interface, where on x86-64 the syscall instruction switches from user-mode (ring 3) to kernel-mode (ring 0) and returns with sysretq (kernel.html).

components.name: RedoxFS
components.note: "This is the default filesystem of Redox OS, inspired by ZFS and adapted to a microkernel architecture."; the page adds "(It's a replacement for TFS)" (RedoxFS).

components.name: pkgar
components.note: Described as "a file format, library, and command-line executable for creating and extracting cryptographically secure collections of files, primarily for use in package management on Redox OS"; the page explains that the name is short for "package archive" (Package Management).

components.name: relibc
components.note: "relibc is a portable C standard library written in Rust and is under heavy development"; the README lists "C, Linux, BSD functions and extensions", a "POSIX compatibility layer" and "Interfaces for system components" (README, github.com/redox-os/relibc).

relations.name: Plan 9 from Bell Labs
relations.note: The Redox OS manual describes a model of resources named by schemes "largely inspired by Plan 9"; Plan 9 remains a distinct system, with no code link to Redox OS.
